role: Address table of the 55 bwx12 kernels: function start, loop start, offset modulo 64.
purpose: build12.sh wrote this table on CRB on 2026-11-15, in the same run that built the runner bwx12 and ran its self-test. Each row gives, for one kernel, the address of its function and of its loop in the binary, and the loop address modulo 64.

main_flow.step: Line 1 is the header. One tab character separates the six columns.
Each later line is one kernel of bwx12. The 55 rows stand in the order of `bwx12 --list`, which is the order of the table `kernels[]` in bwx12.c [Ref4].
Read `start` and `loop_start` as hexadecimal addresses that `objdump` printed for the binary. Read `loop_mod64` as a decimal number.

The bwx12 processes of the whole-chip test (part L, part C and control I) time six of these kernels: `read` (line 2), `asmread` (line 5), `oldread` (line 8), `read_1pl` (line 27), `read_nop96` (line 29) and `read_nop256` (line 39) [Ref6]. They also run `write` (line 3) once per thread before the first interval, and they do not time that call [Ref4].
For the instructions of a kernel open listing.txt in the same folder and find the title line `=== bwx12 <kernel> ===` [Ref2].

behavior_notes: The file holds addresses only. It holds no rate and no time. Whether a loop position changes a rate cannot be read from it.
The old read kernel is the row `oldread` (line 8). The new read kernel is the row `read` (line 2).

The table describes the binary bwx12 only. Part A of the whole-chip test runs the binaries bw_old and bw_new, not bwx12. It times their kernels `read`, `write`, `copy`, `asmread`, `asmwrite` and `asmcopy` [Ref8]. Those functions stand at other addresses [Ref3]. On this page a sentence about which part runs a kernel concerns the function of bwx12 in that row. The same holds for the sentence "The whole-chip test does not run these kernels".

bwx12.c puts unused bytes before each kernel. They set the start of the function, and with it the loop start, to a planned position modulo 64 [Ref4]. For three kernels of the whole-chip test the loop positions of this table equal the loop positions in bw_new and bw_old: `read` 36 and `asmread` 20 as in bw_new, `oldread` 40 as `k_read` of bw_old [Ref3].

Check made for this page on 2026-11-21 with a short Python script on listing.txt and on the saved machine code of bw_new and bw_old: `k_read` and `k_asmread` of bwx12 hold the same instructions as `k_read` and `k_asmread` of bw_new. `k_oldread` of bwx12 holds the same instructions as `k_read` of bw_old. Only the addresses differ [Ref2] [Ref3].
The loops of `read` and `asmread` have the same length (11 instructions, 44 bytes) and different positions: 36 and 20. The `read` loop crosses a 64-byte boundary. The `asmread` loop does not.
The rows are not in the order of the addresses. `oldread` (line 8) has the lowest start address, 0x4600.

No program of the whole-chip test reads this file. check_listing12.py reads it on the development machine. It compares column 6 of each row with the loop start modulo 64 that it computes from listing.txt. For the 29 kernels that bwx11 also has, it compares column 6 with the table of the accepted bwx11 build too. Its saved output check_listing12.out ends with `failed_rows=0` and `new_failed_rows=0` [Ref5].

Check made for this page on 2026-11-21 with a short Python script: in each of the 55 rows `function` is `k_` plus `kernel`, and `loop_mod64` equals `loop_start` modulo 64. The sha256 digest of this file equals the value that build.txt records for it [Ref7].

words.def: the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. On this page "kernel" means this loop. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.
the new read kernel or asmread.
test loops of bwx12: the asmread loop with 96 or 256 no-operation instructions per 256 B, and a loop with one load per 64 B line.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.
the script that builds bwx12 on CRB and writes this file. It stands in the folder above this one.
a command that prints the machine code of a binary as assembler text, one instruction per line with its address.
the file in the same folder that holds the objdump text of every kernel of bwx12.
the build record that build12.sh writes in the same folder: compiler, flags, self-test result and sha256 digests.
a checksum of 256 bits that the command `sha256sum` computes from the content of a file. It is printed as 64 hexadecimal digits.
the first instruction of the loop of a kernel. The backward branch at the end of the loop goes to it.
the remainder after a division by 64. For an address it is the position inside a 64-byte block, from 0 to 63. bwx12.c counts one cache line as 64 bytes.
one run through the instructions of the loop, from the loop start to the backward branch.
the word of build12.sh and check_listing12.py for the build of an earlier version (here bwx11) that serves as the reference for a new build.
the word of build12.sh and check_listing12.py for the machine on which check_listing12.py runs. It is not CRB.
the run under review: the read test with 120 threads on CRB, run on 2026-11-17.
Arm instructions. `ldp` of two q registers loads 32 bytes. `ldr` of a q register loads 16 bytes. `add` adds. `cmp` compares two values for the branch that follows. `nop` does nothing.
the low halves of eight vector registers. A function that changes them must restore them before it returns. The kernel saves them on the stack before the loop and loads them back after it.
a value that the compiled code stores on the stack at the start of a function and compares before the return.
the first write of a thread to its new buffer.
the list of kernel names after the option `--seq` of bwx12. The process times the kernels in this order.

a process is one start of a benchmark binary. An interval is one timed measurement inside a process. bwx12 times a sequence of kernels and repeats the sequence: each repeat is a round (counted from 0), and the position is the place of a kernel in the sequence (counted from 0). In part A the round (1 or 2) is the round of the script: round 2 runs the processes in the reverse order.
the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13, repeated with the same two binaries.
one bwx12 process with the kernel sequence oldread, asmread, read_nop96, read_nop256, read_1pl.
one bwx12 process with the sequence oldread, read, asmread (cfwd) or asmread, read, oldread (crev).
the part L line, started from an idle machine, twice. It was added after the first numbers were seen. It is not part of the plan fixed before the run.
the arguments of one bwx12 process, as a spec file holds them. "The same line" means a process with the same arguments.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.

refs.what: lines 59-75 write this file. Line 60 prints the header. Line 66 takes `start` from the first line of the objdump text. Lines 67-73 find the first backward branch. Line 74 prints the row.
the machine code of the kernels: `read` from line 1, `asmread` from line 59, `oldread` from line 133, `read_1pl` from line 754, `read_nop96` from line 854, `read_nop256` from line 2126.

the machine code of bw_new and bw_old. bw_new `k_read`: the loop starts at 0x1c64 (lines 24-36), 36 modulo 64. bw_new `k_asmread`: 0x1b54 (lines 82-98), 20 modulo 64. bw_old `k_read`: 0x1b68 (lines 156-198), 40 modulo 64.

lines 143-163: the padding before each kernel. Lines 1454-1484: the table `kernels[]`. Line 1646: `worker` calls `k_write` before the first interval. Lines 1663 and 1693-1696: `worker` adds the length of the range of each kernel call to the byte count of the interval (twice the length for a copy kernel). Lines 2921-2924: the option --list.
lines 156-168 read this file and keep column 6. The saved output is check_listing12.out in the same folder as this file.

the kernel sequence of part L and of control I: oldread, asmread, read_nop96, read_nop256, read_1pl. cfwd.spec and crev.spec in the same folder hold the sequences of part C: oldread, read, asmread and asmread, read, oldread.
line 22 holds the sha256 digest of offsets.tsv.
the script of part A. Line 44 names its kernels: read, write, copy, asmread, asmwrite, asmcopy. Lines 39-43 and 45-48 start one process of bw_old and one process of bw_new per kernel and round.
